Reported design prompts, fully worked with the numbers

Every prompt below was reported from a 2026 design round. Each is worked in the same order: the questions that change the design, the options with trade-offs, the numbers (with units written out, because a factor of 8 between bits and bytes is the most common estimation error), the design built up in versions, edge cases and failure handling, and the follow-ups that were asked. The unit conversions and estimation habits are taught in the public appendix, Units and back-of-envelope maths.

Key idea
Network links are quoted in bits per second; storage and memory in bytes. 10 Gb/s (gigabits) = 1.25 GB/s (gigabytes). Convert once, at the start, and write the unit on every number. Then find the bound that no design can beat, and judge each design against it.
In this chapter
  1. Distribute a 500 GB checkpoint to 1,000 GPU workers
  2. Eight GPUs, a large model and a small model
  3. An inference system for document review

  5. Near-duplicate video detection at platform scale

  10. Sharding a feed-forward matmul, with a roofline

Distribute a 500 GB checkpoint to 1,000 GPU workers

Anthropic senior SWE technical screen; Staff onsite "model rollout"; Sr Staff "model downloader"; 2026.

The prompt
A 500 GB checkpoint sits in a central repository with limited egress. 100–1,000 workers (later 10,000) must each receive and verify the full model before the new version serves. Each worker has a 10 Gb/s NIC shared by upload and download. Workers can send to each other. Minimise time to "all workers ready"; handle slow, failed and corrupt transfers; activate and roll back safely.
First minute, out loud
"First the bound: every worker must pull 500 GB, and on average must also upload about that much to peers, through a link of 1.25 gigabytes per second, so nothing beats about 13 minutes. Then I'll show that chunked peer-to-peer gets close to that, while pulling from the source would take days."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Source egress bandwidth?If the source is also 10 Gb/s, it can send each byte only once in 400 s; it must not be the main supplier.
NIC: full duplex or shared?The prompt says shared: each worker moves ~2S through 1.25 GB/s. Full duplex would halve the bound.
Network topology: racks, oversubscribed spine?Prefer in-rack peers; cross-rack traffic is the scarce resource.
Local disk speed; must the model be in GPU memory or on disk?NVMe at ~3 GB/s is not the bottleneck; verifying hashes on one core (~1 GB/s) can be.
Is a coordinator allowed?Simplest; follow-up asks for coordinator-free.
Rollout semantics: all at once, or waves?Waves with rollback need the old version kept on disk.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
All workers pull from the sourceTrivial.N·S ÷ source bandwidth: 1,000 × 500 GB ÷ 1.25 GB/s = 400,000 s ≈ 4.6 days.
Tree (each node forwards to k children)Simple fan-out; log_k N depth.Each internal node uploads k·S: time ≈ (1 + k)·S ÷ b; leaves' upload capacity wasted.
Chunked chain (pipeline)Every link carries 2S once: ≈ 2S ÷ b + N × chunk time.One slow node stalls everyone behind it.
Chunked peer-to-peer (BitTorrent-style)Reaches the bound; routes around slow nodes; scales to 10,000.Needs chunk bookkeeping (tracker or gossip).

Choice: Chunked peer-to-peer with a tracker; describe gossip for the coordinator-free follow-up.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Convert the link10 Gb/s ÷ 8 bits/byte1.25 GB/s per worker, shared up + down
Source boundS ÷ B_src = 500 GB ÷ 1.25 GB/s400 s (source sends each byte once)
Worker bounddownload S + upload ≈ S = 2S through 1.25 GB/s → 1,000 GB ÷ 1.25 GB/s800 s ≈ 13.3 min
Lower boundmax(400 s, 800 s)≈ 13–14 min, independent of N
Naive pull1,000 × 500 GB ÷ 1.25 GB/s400,000 s ≈ 4.6 days
Binary tree, pipelinedeach internal node: receive S + send 2S = 3S ÷ 1.25 GB/s1,200 s + depth × chunk time
Chain, 64 MB chunks2S ÷ b + N × (64 MB ÷ 0.625 GB/s)800 s + 1,000 × 0.1 s ≈ 900 s
Chunks at 256 MB500 GB ÷ 256 MB≈ 1,950 chunks
Manifest1,950 × 32-byte SHA-256 + offsets≈ 100 KB: trivial to send to everyone
Hashing500 GB at ~1 GB/s per core500 s on one core: hash chunks in parallel as they land (8 cores → ~60 s, overlapped)
Tracker load at 10,000 workers10,000 × 1,950 chunk reports ÷ 800 s≈ 24,000 updates/s: batch as bitmaps (1,950 bits ≈ 245 bytes each)

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: chunk and sign. Split into 256 MB chunks; publish a signed manifest of chunk hashes. Workers verify every chunk before using or forwarding it.
  2. v2: tracker-coordinated swarm. Workers report which chunks they hold (bitmaps). Each worker asks the tracker for a few peers holding chunks it lacks, rarest first, preferring the same rack, and keeps 4–8 transfers in flight. The source seeds distinct chunks to many workers first, so every chunk exists in the swarm quickly.
  3. v3: failure handling. Per-chunk timeout; re-request from another peer; a hash mismatch discards the chunk and penalises the peer; a crashed worker restarts from its verified chunks on disk.
  4. v4: activation and rollback. Workers report "verified v42". The controller flips serving in waves (1%, 10%, 100%) with health checks; v41 stays on disk until v42 is healthy everywhere.
  5. v5: no coordinator. Each worker gossips its bitmap to 20–50 random neighbours; requests go to neighbours that advertise the chunk. Converges in O(log N) gossip rounds.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Slow workerIt still downloads at its own pace; peers stop choosing it as a source (track per-peer throughput).
Corrupt chunkHash mismatch → discard, refetch, blacklist after repeats.
Source fails mid-rolloutOnce every chunk has at least one verified copy in the swarm, the source is no longer needed.
Rack uplink saturatedSeed one copy per rack, then distribute within the rack.
Partial activation failureHealth checks stop the wave; roll back to v41.

5 · Complexity and cost

Time ≈ bound + a few chunk times; tracker work O(workers × chunks) updates, batched.

6 · Follow-ups

What lower bound would they expect you to state?

max(S ÷ source bandwidth, 2S ÷ per-worker link) with a shared NIC; S ÷ link with full duplex. The candidate who reported this round thought the bound mattered more than the exact topology.

Same problem inside an RL cluster with RDMA?

That is weight sync: sharded point-to-point copies at ~40 GB/s per GPU (see the RL chapters).

Eight GPUs, a large model and a small model

Anthropic system-design follow-up and "GPU inference scheduler" question, 2026.

The prompt
A pool of 8 GPUs. A small-model batch needs 1 GPU; a large-model batch needs all 8 at once. Both take the same time t. Requests for both arrive continuously. Design the scheduler.
First minute, out loud
"First check the load fits: a large batch costs 8 GPU-time units, a small one 1. Then the real problem is the drain: to start a large batch I must wait for all eight to be free, and every small job I admit meanwhile delays it, while every GPU I leave idle wastes capacity."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Arrival rates and SLAs for each class?Decides priority and how long large requests may wait.
Can small jobs be preempted?If yes, drain is instant at the cost of wasted work.
Can requests be batched (several large requests per drain)?Amortises the drain cost.
Is t really fixed, or does it vary?Variable t makes backfilling predictions uncertain.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
FIFO, one queueSimple.A large request at the head blocks small ones behind it while GPUs idle.
Strict priority to largeLarge latency low.Stops admitting small jobs on every large arrival: idle GPUs during each drain.
Reservation + backfill (EASY backfilling)Large requests get a guaranteed start time; small jobs fill gaps only if they finish before it.Needs runtime estimates.
Time-division (periodic large slots)Predictable for both classes.Wastes a slot when no large work is queued.

Choice: Two queues; reservation with backfill; batch large requests per drain with a maximum wait from the SLA; time-division when both classes are heavy.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Stability condition(8·λ_L·t + λ_S·t) ÷ 8 < 1must hold or no scheduler helps
Example load, t = 1 sλ_L = 0.05/s, λ_S = 4/s → (0.4 + 4) ÷ 8utilisation 0.55
Drain waste if admission stops when a large request arrivesother 7 GPUs finish at uniform random times in [0, t]: expected idle = 7 × t/2≈ 3.5 GPU-seconds per drain
Same, batching L = 4 large requests per drain3.5 ÷ 4≈ 0.9 GPU-s per large batch
Large-request waitdrain (≤ t) + queue≈ 0.5–1 s at this load; grows sharply as utilisation → 1

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: two queues and the gang rule. Large batches take all 8 GPUs atomically: never partial allocation (two large jobs holding 4 each would deadlock).
  2. v2: reservation. When a large request is at the head, compute when 8 GPUs will be free; stop starting small jobs that would end after that time.
  3. v3: batching and aging. Hold large requests up to a size or a maximum wait derived from their SLA; age small requests so they cannot starve either.
  4. v4: heavy mixed load. Fixed cycle: one large slot every P seconds sized to λ_L, small work otherwise.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Steady stream of small jobsReservation prevents large starvation.
No large requests for a long timeTime-division slots are released to small work.
A GPU failsPool of 7 cannot run large batches: alert and route large requests elsewhere.

5 · Complexity and cost

Scheduler decisions O(log n) per event.

6 · Follow-ups

At cluster scale?

Gang scheduling with Kueue or Slurm, plus preemption policies.

An inference system for document review

Anthropic system-design round, 2026 (drilled on cache hit rate, batching and load balancing).

The prompt
Design an inference system where users ask many questions about long documents. The interviewer asked how to measure cache hit rate, which batching strategy to use, and how to load-balance requests before the GPUs.
First minute, out loud
"Each request repeats a long prefix: instructions, rubric, the document. If that prefix's KV cache is reused, prefill shrinks to the question. So routing decides cost: send every question about a document to the replica that already holds it."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Documents per day, length, questions per document, arrival pattern?Sets prefill volume and how much reuse is possible.
Latency target: interactive or batch?Interactive needs headroom; batch can wait for big batches.
Model size?Sets KV bytes per token and how many documents fit in cache.
Do the questions about one document arrive together?If they are spread over hours, the cache must persist longer (CPU or SSD tier).

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Round-robin load balancingEven load.Each replica re-prefills the same document: hit rate collapses.
Consistent hashing by document idHigh hit rate; losing a replica moves only its keys.Hot documents overload one replica.
Hash + bounded load (spill to next on the ring)High hit rate and bounded queues.A little more logic.

Choice: Consistent hashing on document id with bounded load; continuous batching with chunked prefill inside each engine; separate interactive and bulk queues.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Workload (assumed)1M docs/day × 20 questions; doc 8,000 tokens + rubric 1,000 + question 100; answer 30020M requests/day
Prefill tokens, no reuse20M × 9,100182B tokens/day = 2.1M tokens/s
Prefill tokens, document cached1M × 9,100 + 20M × 10011.1B tokens/day = 128K tokens/s (16× less)
Decode tokens20M × 3006B tokens/day = 69K tokens/s
KV cache per token, 8B model (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dims, BF16)2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes131 KB/token
KV for one document prefix9,000 tokens × 131 KB≈ 1.2 GB
Documents resident per 80 GB H100(80 − 16 GB weights − headroom) ≈ 55 GB ÷ 1.2 GB≈ 45 documents
Hit rate with all 20 questions on one replicacached prompt tokens ÷ prompt tokens = (19 × 9,000) ÷ (20 × 9,100)≈ 94%
GPUs for prefill (≈ 25K tokens/s per H100 for 8B)128K ÷ 25K vs 2.1M ÷ 25K≈ 5 vs ≈ 84 GPUs
GPUs for decode (≈ 8K tokens/s per H100 at batch 64)69K ÷ 8K≈ 9 GPUs; double everything for peaks

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: one replica. vLLM with prefix caching; measure prefix-cache hit rate from engine counters.
  2. v2: many replicas, affinity routing. Router hashes document id to a replica; spill to the next replica on the ring when its queue exceeds a bound.
  3. v3: batching. Continuous batching; chunked prefill so long prefills do not stall decoding; interactive traffic prioritised over bulk.
  4. v4: cache tiers. If questions about a document are spread out, offload KV blocks to CPU memory or SSD and reload instead of re-prefilling.
  5. v5: measure. Report hit rate per replica and by prefix level, cost per reviewed document, p50/p99 latency per class.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Hot documentBounded-load spill; replicate hot prefixes on two replicas.
Replica diesConsistent hashing moves only its documents; they re-prefill once.
Document updatedNew hash (content hash in the key) avoids stale cache.

5 · Complexity and cost

Cost is proportional to uncached prefill tokens plus generated tokens; affinity routing is the 16× lever here.

6 · Follow-ups

How do you measure cache hit rate correctly?

Token-weighted (cached prompt tokens ÷ prompt tokens), per replica and overall; request-weighted hit rate hides that the misses are the expensive long prefixes.

A 1,000-page document to structured text: CPU, GPU and memory stages

Mistral senior SWE system design, 2026.

The prompt
Design an API that converts a roughly 1,000-page document into structured text through three stages: CPU-heavy page rendering, GPU-heavy recognition, and memory-heavy transformation.
First minute, out loud
"It is a pipeline of three resource types, so I size each stage to the same throughput and put bounded queues between them. The interesting numbers are bytes per page between stages: an uncompressed page image is about 26 megabytes."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Target throughput and latency per document?Throughput sizes pools; latency decides whether pages of one document run in parallel.
Page image resolution and format?Sets bytes between stages.
Synchronous API or job + callback?1,000 pages takes minutes: return a job id.
Can stages share a machine?Co-locating render and GPU avoids shipping images over the network.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
One worker does all three stages per documentSimple.GPU idles during rendering; memory spikes.
Stage pools with queuesEach resource sized independently; back-pressure.More moving parts.
Co-located render + GPU, separate transformNo image traffic over the network.Less flexible scaling.

Choice: Asynchronous jobs; per-page tasks through three pools with bounded queues; co-locate render and recognition if image bandwidth dominates.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Target (assumed)100 documents/hour × 1,000 pages100,000 pages/hour ≈ 28 pages/s
Render (assume 0.2 core-s/page)28 × 0.2≈ 6 cores
Recognition (assume 0.05 GPU-s/page, batched)28 × 0.05≈ 1.4 → 2 GPUs
Page image, 300 DPI A4 RGB2,480 × 3,508 × 3 bytes≈ 26 MB uncompressed (≈ 2–3 MB PNG)
Render → GPU bandwidth, raw28 pages/s × 26 MB≈ 730 MB/s ≈ 5.8 Gb/s (most of a 10 Gb/s NIC)
Same, PNG28 × 3 MB≈ 84 MB/s ≈ 0.7 Gb/s
Transform memory (assume 50 MB/page in flight)queue bound 200 pages × 50 MB≈ 10 GB

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: job API. POST /documents returns a job id; the client polls or receives a webhook; results stored per page then assembled.
  2. v2: per-page tasks and three pools. Split into page tasks; render pool (CPU), recognition pool (GPU, batches of pages), transform pool (memory-heavy machines). Bounded queues give back-pressure.
  3. v3: bandwidth. Send compressed images between stages, or co-locate render and GPU on the same host.
  4. v4: reliability. Idempotent page tasks keyed by (doc, page, stage); retries; a page that keeps failing is marked and the document completes with a gap report.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
One huge page (fold-out map)Tile it.
Scanned vs digital PDFDigital: extract text directly, skip recognition.
Burst of large documentsQueues absorb; autoscale the GPU pool on queue depth.

5 · Complexity and cost

Throughput = the slowest stage; latency ≈ pages ÷ parallelism + per-page latency.

6 · Follow-ups

What would make this a scheduling problem?

Mixed priorities and a fixed GPU pool: the same reservation and batching ideas as the eight-GPU question.

Near-duplicate video detection at platform scale

Google senior MLE ML-design round, 2026.

The prompt
Detect visually similar or duplicate videos on a large short-video platform. The interviewer pushed on embeddings, compression, high-concurrency search, false positives, human review, and quantitatively trading embedding quality against latency.
First minute, out loud
"Embed each video into a few vectors, index them with approximate nearest-neighbour search, check new uploads against the index, and verify close matches with a more precise frame-level comparison. The numbers decide compression: a billion float vectors do not fit in memory, product-quantised ones do."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Corpus size and upload rate?Sizes the index and query rate.
What counts as duplicate: re-uploads, crops, mirrored, re-encoded, compilations?Decides the embedding's invariances and whether frame-level matching is needed.
Action on a match: block, demote, send to review?Sets the precision you need.
Latency budget at upload?Synchronous check vs asynchronous.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Perceptual hashes per frameCheap, exact-ish duplicates.Weak on crops and edits.
Learned embeddings + ANNRobust to edits.Index memory; false positives on similar content.
Two-stage: ANN recall, then frame alignment verificationHigh precision.Extra compute on candidates only.

Choice: Learned keyframe embeddings, IVF-PQ or HNSW index sharded in memory, verification stage, human review for the uncertain band.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Corpus (assumed)1B videos × 8 keyframe embeddings8B vectors
Raw size, 512-d float328B × 512 × 4 bytes16 TB: does not fit in RAM
Product-quantised to 64 bytes8B × 64 bytes512 GB: ~8 servers with 64+ GB free each
Upload rate (assumed)50M/day ÷ 86,400 s≈ 580 queries/s, ~2,000/s peak, × 8 keyframes
Review loadif 0.1% of uploads are uncertain: 50M × 0.00150,000 reviews/day

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: embeddings. Sample keyframes, embed with a model trained for invariance to crops, re-encoding and overlays (contrastive training on augmented pairs).
  2. v2: index. IVF-PQ or HNSW, sharded by vector id; query all shards in parallel and merge top-k.
  3. v3: verify. For candidates above a similarity threshold, align frame sequences (temporal matching) to confirm.
  4. v4: decide. High confidence: automatic action; middle band: human review; log decisions as labels to retrain.
  5. v5: quality vs latency. Sweep PQ code size and ANN parameters; plot recall@k against p99 latency and memory; pick the knee.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Mirrored or cropped copiesAugment training pairs with these transforms.
Legitimately similar content (same meme template)Verification stage plus policy on what counts as duplicate.
Index drift after embedding model updateRe-embed in the background; dual-write to old and new index during migration.

5 · Complexity and cost

Index memory ∝ vectors × code size; query latency ∝ probes × shard size.

6 · Follow-ups

How do you evaluate?

Labelled duplicate pairs: precision and recall at the operating threshold, measured separately per transform type; review-queue precision online.

1:1 messaging for 100 million daily users

Anthropic Staff backend system-design screen; Sr Staff "1:1 chat"; 2026.

The prompt
Web-only direct messaging (no groups, no media, no push). 100M daily active users. Offline recipients get messages when they return. Follow-ups: ordering, deduplication, routing between servers, replication lag, spikes.
First minute, out loud
"Messages are tiny; the scale problem is connections, not bytes. About 30 million open WebSockets, a presence map from user to gateway, persist-then-deliver, and per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering and catch-up."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Messages per user per day? Peak ratio?Sets write QPS.
Ordering guarantee: per conversation, or global?Per conversation is enough and much cheaper.
Delivery semantics?At-least-once plus client-side dedup by message id.
Retention?Storage growth.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Single queue for all messagesSimple.Bottleneck; the reported candidate who started here felt pushed toward pub/sub.
Pub/sub channel per gateway serverEach gateway subscribes to its own channel; senders publish to the recipient's gateway.Needs the presence map.
Channel per userSimple routing.100M channels: heavy for most brokers.

Choice: Gateways hold WebSockets; presence map (user → gateway) in Redis; persist to a store partitioned by conversation; publish to the recipient gateway's channel.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Messages (assumed 40/user/day)100M × 404B/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 46K/s avg, ~140K/s peak (×3)
Stored bytes (≈ 300 B per message with metadata)4B × 300 B1.2 TB/day; × 3 replicas = 3.6 TB/day ≈ 1.3 PB/year
Write bandwidth at peak140K/s × 300 B42 MB/s ≈ 336 Mb/s: small
Concurrent connections (30% online)0.3 × 100M30M WebSockets
Gateways at ~200K connections each30M ÷ 200K≈ 150 servers (plus headroom)

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: send path. Client → gateway → message service: assign per-conversation sequence number, persist (quorum write), ack sender, then route.
  2. v2: delivery. Look up recipient's gateway in presence; publish to that gateway's channel; gateway pushes over the WebSocket. Offline: nothing to push; message waits in storage.
  3. v3: catch-up. On reconnect the client sends its last sequence number per conversation; server returns the gap.
  4. v4: dedup and ordering. Client-generated message id with a unique constraint (idempotent retries); clients order by sequence number.
  5. v5: spikes and lag. Queue between gateway and message service absorbs spikes; reads of just-written messages go to the leader or use the sequence number to detect lag.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Recipient connected to two tabsPresence maps user → set of gateways.
Gateway diesClients reconnect elsewhere and catch up by sequence number.
Sender retries after timeoutMessage id dedup.
Hot conversationPartition key is conversation id: one hot partition; rare for 1:1.

5 · Complexity and cost

Write O(1) per message; connection count drives gateway fleet size.

6 · Follow-ups

Why sequence numbers per conversation?

Ordering only matters within a conversation, and a per-conversation counter avoids a global sequencer.

A secure sandboxed cloud IDE

OpenAI senior SWE system design, 2026.

The prompt
Browser-based IDE: users create workspaces, edit files, open terminals, run and build code on provider machines. Arbitrary, possibly hostile code. Workspaces outlive short-lived sandboxes; idle ones are suspended. Run and Build logs stream live and survive reconnects. A host failure may lose at most about one minute of work.
First minute, out loud
"Hostile code means a container sharing the host kernel is not enough: microVMs with default-deny egress. The one-minute loss budget means snapshotting dirty files every minute to object storage, and that sets the bandwidth."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Concurrent active workspaces and machine size each?Fleet size.
Typical write rate per workspace?Snapshot bandwidth.
Network access for user code?Package mirrors only, or full internet with abuse controls.
Resume time target?Warm pools vs cold boot.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Containers (runc)Fast, dense.Shared kernel: one kernel exploit escapes.
gVisorSyscall interception; better isolation.Some syscalls slow or missing.
microVMs (Firecracker)VM-grade isolation, ~125 ms boot.Less density than containers.

Choice: Firecracker microVMs on dedicated hosts, default-deny egress, per-minute dirty-file snapshots to object storage.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Concurrent workspaces (assumed)10,000 × 2 vCPU, 4 GB20,000 vCPU, 40 TB RAM
Hosts at 64 vCPU / 256 GB with 75% packing20,000 ÷ (64 × 0.75)≈ 420 hosts
Snapshot traffic (10 MB dirty per workspace per minute)10,000 × 10 MB ÷ 60 s≈ 1.7 GB/s ≈ 13 Gb/s to object storage
Per host13 Gb/s ÷ 420≈ 32 Mb/s: easy on a 25 Gb/s NIC

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: control plane. Workspace service (metadata), scheduler (place microVMs), storage (object store for files, snapshots).
  2. v2: session. Start or resume a microVM from a warm pool; mount the workspace from local disk restored from the latest snapshot.
  3. v3: durability. Track dirty files; every minute upload changed files (content-addressed); on host failure restore on another host from the last snapshot.
  4. v4: jobs and logs. Run/Build are tracked jobs; logs stream through a log service (append-only, per job), so a reconnecting browser resumes from an offset.
  5. v5: security. Default-deny egress, per-workspace resource limits, no metadata-service access, image allow-list.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Fork bomb or disk fillcgroup limits; kill and report.
Crypto miningCPU quotas and anomaly detection.
Browser disconnect during buildJob keeps running; logs persisted.

5 · Complexity and cost

Fleet ∝ concurrent workspaces; snapshot bandwidth ∝ write rate.

6 · Follow-ups

Why not snapshot the whole VM?

Full memory snapshots are GBs per workspace; files-only snapshots meet the one-minute budget at a fraction of the bytes.

A collaborative prompt playground

Anthropic onsite design round (several reports), 2026.

The prompt
Users edit prompts together, run them against models, compare outputs, and keep versions. Follow-ups reported: storing large prompt revisions efficiently, collaboration, execution.
First minute, out loud
"Three parts: a document with concurrent editing, an immutable revision history, and asynchronous runs whose results are keyed by (revision, model, parameters) so they can be cached and compared."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Real-time co-editing or turn-based?CRDT/OT vs locks.
Prompt size and revisions per prompt?Storage: full copies vs deltas.
Run volume and model cost?Rate limits, quotas, caching of identical runs.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Full copy per revisionSimple reads.Storage grows with size × revisions.
Delta chain with periodic full snapshotsSmall storage; fast enough reads.Reconstruct cost.
Content-addressed chunksDeduplicates shared text across prompts.More complex.

Choice: Delta chain with a full snapshot every N revisions; CRDT for live editing; content-addressed run cache.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Revisions (assumed)1M prompts × 50 revisions × 4 KB200 GB as full copies
Deltas (≈ 10% of size) + snapshot every 101M × (5 × 4 KB + 45 × 0.4 KB)≈ 38 GB
Runs (assumed 2M/day, 1 KB in + 2 KB out stored)2M × 3 KB6 GB/day

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: data model. Prompt (id, owner, ACL), Revision (id, parent, delta or snapshot), Run (revision, model, params hash, status, output).
  2. v2: collaboration. CRDT (Yjs-style) for the editor; commit a revision on explicit save or idle.
  3. v3: execution. Runs are jobs on a queue with per-workspace rate limits; stream output to the UI; cache by (revision, model, params, seed).
  4. v4: compare. Side-by-side outputs for two revisions or models; optional judge scoring.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Concurrent savesRevisions form a DAG; show branches.
Very large prompts (with documents)Store attachments separately by hash.
Non-deterministic outputsCache only when temperature is 0 or the seed is fixed.

5 · Complexity and cost

Storage ∝ deltas; run cost dominates.

6 · Follow-ups

Evaluate prompt changes?

Run both revisions on a fixed test set and compare with paired statistics (public guide, eval statistics).

ChatGPT, simplified: streaming and the client

OpenAI SWE onsite and full-stack (safety team) phone screen, 2026.

The prompt
Design a simplified ChatGPT. Interviewers said to skip large-scale architecture and persistence, then asked: why Server-Sent Events rather than WebSockets; how a new chat gets its title; auto-scroll when tokens arrive while the user reads older messages; rendering very long conversations.
First minute, out loud
"The server side is a request to the model with the conversation, streamed back token by token. The interesting parts are on the client: a stream that survives proxies, a title generated after the first exchange, and a scroll position that respects the reader."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Multiple devices open at once?Sync state through the server.
Stop / regenerate?Abort the stream server-side.
Expected concurrent streams?Egress bandwidth and connection count.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Server-Sent EventsOne-way, plain HTTP, proxy-friendly, auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID.Text only; one direction.
WebSocketsBidirectional.Heavier; some proxies interfere; not needed for one-way streaming.
Long pollingUniversal.Latency and overhead.

Choice: SSE for responses; normal POSTs for user actions.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Concurrent streams (assumed)1M—
Tokens per stream≈ 50 tokens/s50M events/s
Bytes per SSE event≈ 30 bytes (data: prefix, token, newlines)50M × 30 B = 1.5 GB/s ≈ 12 Gb/s egress

3 · Build it step by step

  1. v1: send. POST message; server appends to conversation and opens an SSE stream of tokens.
  2. v2: title. Sidebar shows "New chat"; after the first response completes, a small model call produces a title and the server pushes the update.
  3. v3: scroll. Auto-scroll only if the user is within a few pixels of the bottom; otherwise show a "new messages" button.
  4. v4: long conversations. Virtualised list (render visible messages only); incremental markdown rendering for the streaming message.
  5. v5: stop and reconnect. Abort endpoint cancels generation; reconnect with Last-Event-ID resumes from the buffered position.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Network drop mid-streamReconnect and resume from the last event id.
User edits an earlier messageBranch the conversation.
Very long single answerRender incrementally; throttle DOM updates to animation frames.

5 · Complexity and cost

Egress ∝ concurrent streams × tokens/s × bytes per event.

6 · Follow-ups

Why did the full-stack interviewer care about scroll?

Product behaviour under streaming is where real bugs live; it tests whether you think about the user, not only the backend.

Sharding a feed-forward matmul, with a roofline

Anthropic infra onsite ML-systems round (spreadsheet tool), 2026.

The prompt
For a transformer feed-forward block, compare sharding strategies across 8 GPUs using a roofline-style model: compute time, communication time, and which is the bottleneck.
First minute, out loud
"Two numbers per strategy: compute time is FLOPs divided by achievable FLOP/s; communication time is bytes moved divided by link bandwidth. The good sharding is the one where communication is small next to compute."

1 · Questions to ask before building

AskWhy it changes the solution
Model width d, hidden 4d, tokens per step B, precision?Every number follows from these.
Interconnect: NVLink within a node or network across nodes?450 GB/s vs ~50 GB/s per GPU changes the answer by 9×.
Forward only, or forward and backward?Backward roughly doubles both terms.

2 · Approaches, pros and cons

ApproachProsCons
Column-parallel W1, row-parallel W2 (Megatron)One all-reduce of [B, d] per block.Activations replicated before the block.
Shard the contracting dimension of W1Simple to describe.All-reduce of [B, 4d]: four times the bytes.
Data parallel onlyNo activation communication.Full weights per GPU; gradient all-reduce instead.

Choice: Megatron column-then-row inside a node.

The numbers

QuantityArithmeticResult
Shapesd = 8,192, 4d = 32,768, B = 4,096 tokens, BF16 (2 bytes)—
FLOPs, forward, both matmuls2 × B × d × 4d × 2≈ 4.4 × 10¹² FLOPs
Per GPU (8-way)4.4 × 10¹² ÷ 85.5 × 10¹¹ FLOPs
Compute time at 50% of 989 TFLOP/s5.5 × 10¹¹ ÷ 4.9 × 10¹⁴≈ 1.1 ms
Megatron all-reduce sizeB × d × 2 bytes67 MB
Ring all-reduce bytes per GPU2 × (n − 1)/n × 67 MB = 1.75 × 67 MB117 MB
Comm time on NVLink 450 GB/s117 MB ÷ 450 GB/s≈ 0.26 ms (24% of compute)
Contracting-dim sharding all-reduceB × 4d × 2 bytes = 268 MB → 1.75 × 268 MB ÷ 450 GB/s≈ 1.04 ms (≈ compute: bad)
Megatron across nodes at 50 GB/s117 MB ÷ 50 GB/s≈ 2.3 ms (2× compute: keep tensor parallel inside a node)

3 · Build it step by step

  1. Write the shapes and the per-GPU FLOPs. Divide by achievable, not peak, FLOP/s (30–50% in practice).
  2. Write the bytes each strategy moves. Use the ring all-reduce factor 2(n − 1)/n.
  3. Compare and overlap. Communication below ~30% of compute can be overlapped with the next matmul; above compute, the strategy is wrong for this link.

4 · Edge cases

CaseHandling
Small B (decode)Compute shrinks with B but weights still stream: memory-bound; the roofline intensity ≈ B.
Across nodes9× slower links: use pipeline or data parallelism across nodes instead.

5 · Complexity and cost

Compute ∝ B·d²/n; communication ∝ B·d for Megatron.

6 · Follow-ups

Where is the ridge point?

Peak FLOP/s ÷ HBM bandwidth ≈ 295 FLOP/byte on an H100: a weight matmul with B below that is memory-bound.
